newsitem.title: POLAND: Pope's Polish visit heartens Roman Catholic right.
newsitem.headline: Pope's Polish visit heartens Roman Catholic right.

text.p: Pope John Paul's emotional visit to his homeland has given heart to the Polish Church's rightist allies in their battle for votes with the ruling ex-communists.
"This pilgrimage could very much strengthen the mobilising force of the Church in society," said Lena Kolarska-Bobinska, a sociologist heading the Institute of Public Affairs thinktank.
"I think this could help the right," she told Reuters.
The Roman Catholic Church estimates six million people, many young and often deeply moved, attended events of the 11-day pilgrimage which ended on Tuesday -- two million more than expected.
They heard the Pope, while avoiding involvement in party politics, uncompromisingly condemn abortion and stress Christianity's central role in Polish life.

This could look ominous for the Democratic Left Alliance of former communists, which proclaims liberal secular values as it battles a challenge from the opposition Solidarity Election Action grouping at elections due in September.
The crowds showed Polish Catholicism is vibrant despite a decrease in its authority since the fall of communism in 1989.

The Church was widely respected when, with the Pope's support from the Vatican and in his homecomings of 1979, 1983 and 1987, it championed human rights and the Solidarity free trade union's struggle under communist rule.
The mood shifted under democratic cabinets, partly due to secular attitudes from the West and to resentment over the Church's political forays to back its views and interests.

"This pilgrimage...shows the end of the crisis of identity of the Polish Church, Polish religiousness, Polish patriotism, which was seen after 1989 among many people," Marian Pilka, head of a pro-Church opposition party told Reuters.
"This will have an indirect political impact," said Pilka of the Christian National Alliance, an AWS member party.
The ex-communists have so far bet that defying the Church is a vote winner -- analysts say it probably contributed to their 1993 election victory over a Solidarity-rooted cabinet.

Not only did ex-communists back a liberalised law on abortion last year, they are now delaying ratification by parliament of a 1993 concordat treaty signed with the Vatican to regulate the Church's role in areas such as education.
They clashed head-on with the right and Church over Poland's new constitution, narrowly passed in a May referendum.
The ex-communists' careful handling of the Papal visit was a showpiece of damage control by a party which includes some outspoken anti-clericalists.

Their leaders constantly hailed his words. President Aleksander Kwasniewski had more opportunity to be pictured with the Pope, talking respectfully, than Solidarity leader Marian Krzaklewski who was publicly blessed at a mass.

Even when the Pope thundered against ideas they support, especially on abortion, ex-communist commentators avoided open controversy and instead spoke of his unifying, apolitical approach, contrasting it with that of bishops in Poland.
They took his call for walls dividing Europe to come down as backing for their drive to enter the European Union, which some churchmen see as a possible threat to national identity.
The left is sticking to its policies, hoping Poles will distinguish between religious belief and voting intentions.
"They can pray fervently and vote sensibly," Trybuna daily, linked with the main ruling party, wrote on Wednesday.
But sociologist Kolarska-Bobinska said the left may now tone down its stress on abortion rights, while some critics of the right hope the Pope's influence will cool its rhetoric.
"Let's hope this will calm things, curb the aggressiveness of those who think they have the full authority of the Church," Henryk Wujec, a centrist opposition deputy, told Radio Zet.
Both bishops and ex-communists saw hopeful signs for future understanding in their cooperation to organise the trip and in the relative political calm while the Pope was present.

"This was a Poland of good coexistence of Church and state. This was like a special concordat signed by facts and ratified by life," Poland's Cardinal Jozef Glemp said in a farewell speech before the Pope flew back to the Vatican.
